summary.text: For each threshold \(k>1\), excluded middle is applied to the assertion that values at least \(k\) occur at arbitrarily large indices. If this assertion fails, its negation yields a bound \(N\) beyond which every value is less than \(k\), giving the stated finite/infinite dichotomy.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(n)=\min\{d:d\text{ is a decimal digit occurring in }n^3\}.
\]
For \(n=0\), take \(a(0)=0\), in agreement with the usual decimal representation. The formal statement proved is the following:

> For every natural number \(k>1\), either there is a natural number \(N\) such that
> \[
> n\ge N\implies a(n)<k,
> \]
> or, for every natural number \(M\), there is a natural number \(n\ge M\) such that
> \[
> a(n)\ge k.
> \]

Fix a natural number \(k>1\). Consider the proposition
\[
P_k:\qquad \text{for every }M\in\mathbb N\text{ there is an }n\in\mathbb N
\text{ such that }n\ge M\text{ and }a(n)\ge k.
\]
By the law of excluded middle, either \(P_k\) is true or it is false.

If \(P_k\) is true, then its assertion is exactly the second alternative of the theorem: occurrences of values \(a(n)\ge k\) can be found beyond every prescribed bound \(M\).

Now suppose that \(P_k\) is false. Negating its quantified assertion gives
\[
\exists N\in\mathbb N\;\forall n\in\mathbb N,
\quad \neg\bigl(N\le n\ \text{and}\ k\le a(n)\bigr).
\]
Choose such an \(N\). We claim that every \(n\ge N\) satisfies \(a(n)<k\). Indeed, let \(n\) be any natural number with \(N\le n\). If one also had \(k\le a(n)\), then both parts of
\[
N\le n\quad\text{and}\quad k\le a(n)
\]
would hold, contrary to the defining property of \(N\). Hence \(k\nleq a(n)\). Since the natural numbers are linearly ordered, \(k\nleq a(n)\) is equivalent to \(a(n)<k\). Thus
\[
\forall n\in\mathbb N,\qquad N\le n\implies a(n)<k,
\]
which is exactly the first alternative.

These two cases prove the stated dichotomy for the chosen \(k\), and since \(k>1\) was arbitrary, they prove it for every natural number \(k>1\). Notice that neither the hypothesis \(k>1\) nor any special property of decimal digits or cubes is needed for this dichotomy; it holds for every natural-number-valued sequence.

For clarity about its relation to the OEIS question, taking \(k=2\) makes the second alternative say that for every \(M\) there is an \(n\ge M\) with \(a(n)\ge2\), equivalently that infinitely many \(n\) satisfy \(a(n)>1\). However, the proved statement does not establish that this second alternative holds: it allows instead the first alternative, namely that eventually every \(a(n)<2\). Thus the accepted formal statement is a bounded-versus-unbounded logical dichotomy, not by itself a resolution of the stronger conjecture that infinitely many \(n\) have \(a(n)>1\).
